analysis.one_liner: Repeals the entire Affordable Care Act and its companion health and education law.
analysis.headline: The repeal bill, introduced by Representative Steve King with one cosponsor 17 days before the Congress ended, was referred to eight committees and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 retroactive to their enactment, and restore every prior law they changed. That would take away the ACA's insurance rules, coverage expansions, and subsidies and put pre-2010 health and student-loan law back in place. It was introduced two weeks before the 111th Congress expired, referred to eight committees, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, health insurers would be freed from the ACA's rules requiring them to cover sick applicants, spend a set share of premiums on care, and ban lifetime coverage caps. Drug makers would regain freedom from the law's cost-containment and biosimilar provisions. The bill has no replacement, so anyone who would have gained coverage or subsidies under the ACA loses instead.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and the 2010 reconciliation act effective as of their enactment, wiping them from the books as if they never existed.
Restores or revives every provision of law the two acts amended or repealed, returning federal health and education law to its pre-2010 state.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people: the millions who would lose or never gain the ACA's protections — guaranteed coverage for preexisting conditions, an end to lifetime benefit caps, young-adult coverage, subsidies for lower-income buyers — plus student borrowers, since the reconciliation act changed federal student lending.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sick people and new coverage seekers

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals with no replacement, so consumer protections that were already in effect or scheduled — coverage for preexisting conditions, an end to lifetime dollar caps on benefits, premium-review rules — would vanish and prior law would be restored.
Retroactive repeal effective as of enactment would create legal chaos: taxes paid, subsidies issued, and contracts written under the two laws would all be unwound by a single sentence.
It also repeals the education half of the reconciliation act, upending the federal student-loan system overhaul that was already in motion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers only removal, not reform: everything the ACA did, good and bad, is stripped away with nothing in its place. Its practical benefit is limited to industries freed from the law's rules; its cost falls on people who had just gained or were about to gain coverage and protections. It also carries the administrative shock of retroactive repeal. Even the bill's own backers introduced it knowing it had two sponsors and 17 days left in the session.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to eight committees in its first week and sat there until the Congress ended 17 days later, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Steve King of Iowa introduced the bill on December 17, 2010, joined by Representative Michele Bachmann as its only cosponsor.

That same day it was referred to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Appropriations, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, and Rules — none took it up.
No further action was taken before the 111th Congress expired on January 3, 2011, so the bill died without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People covered by or waiting on the ACA's protections — guaranteed issue for preexisting conditions, the end of lifetime benefit caps, dependent coverage for young adults — were better off because the repeal never advanced. The 111th Congress expired before any committee or chamber acted on it.

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full repeal of the ACA and the 2010 reconciliation act.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration in the final weeks of the session.

sides.party_line_note: Only two House Republicans ever put their names on it — the sponsor and one cosponsor out of 178 — and no Democrat supported it; there was never a vote to split on.

industries.note: Full repeal would free insurers from guaranteed-issue, medical-loss-ratio, and lifetime-cap rules, letting them return to the pre-2010 practice of declining or limiting coverage for sick customers. It would also strip away the individual mandate that brought them millions of new customers, so the gain is deregulation without the offsetting revenue.

Repeal would remove the ACA's coverage expansions and its pathway for lower-cost biosimilars and cost-measures that pressure drug prices, leaving drug makers with a larger market for full-price products. Consumers would pay the difference.
Repealing the reconciliation act undoes its overhaul of federal student lending along with its health provisions, reinstating the pre-2010 loan system and its terms.
